reviewer: Independent integration subagent, direct image inspection
scope: Qualitative observations of the actual files listed; no blind human ratings or universal quality score. H1/H2/H3 are development outputs, not terminal benchmark evidence.
causalAttribution: No controlled causal improvement claim. H3 has a different output resolution and structural changes in addition to appearance changes.
historicalReproducibility: H1 and H2 output files are retained; their earlier code snapshots were not available in the reviewed core report.

notes: The apple, pear and orange are recognizable, but smooth silhouettes, simple stems and broad uniform highlights give a rendered illustration appearance.
Contact shadows are very shallow and the fruit-to-table relationship looks weak.
Fruit surface variation is more prominent than the H1 viewed image, but the yellow-green pear has large repeated stripe-like lobes and the orange shows large blotches.
The additional surface variation does not establish photographic material behavior; silhouettes and simple lighting remain conspicuous.
Snowy mountain and water layers are identifiable, but near-vertical edge discontinuities and repeated tree silhouettes are plainly visible.
Foreground trees, rocks and lake reflections do not form a convincing contact/occlusion arrangement.
The viewed landscape retains the sharp layer discontinuity near the left mountain edge and repeated tree patterns.
More rock texture does not resolve the geometric grounding or the flat mountain-layer appearance.
Pole, horizontal support and signal are connected in the inspected view.
Repeated simple window frames and dark glass stripes, very uniform wall response, simplified signal glyphs and a sparse pavement pattern still look procedural.
The pole base and wall-ground relationship lack the rich contact and material detail visible in a natural photo.
The large left mountain discontinuity visible in the earlier viewed landscape is reduced, and shoreline objects are more clearly arranged.
Repeated tree silhouettes, broad flat mountain layers, synthetic snow patches and near-mirrored lake patterns still give a generated illustration appearance.
The foreground rock edge and ground contact remain weak.
The pear silhouette and surface variation are less striped than the H2 viewed result.
Fruit remain recognizable, but broad soft highlights, simplified stem attachment and shallow contact shadows do not yet resemble a high-quality photographic still life.
